passage:
There was a folded note on my desk on Monday morning. Seema, in her tiny handwriting: "Thanks for saying something on Friday." That's all. She didn't look at me all day, and I didn't look at her, but I think we both knew.
The funny part is that all I said to the boys at the gate was, "Leave her alone, it's not that deep." My voice wobbled. I honestly thought it barely counted. But Seema told me later that what stayed with her was that somebody turned around and saw her.
I'm Leela, and what I learned is that you don't need a big speech. Sometimes being seen matters more. So I said, "You're welcome." That was enough.

qa.q: What did Seema write on the folded note?
qa.a: She wrote, "Thanks for saying something on Friday."

qa.q: What did Leela think of the words Leela said at the gate?
qa.a: Leela thought they barely counted, because Leela's voice wobbled and all Leela said was 'Leave her alone, it's not that deep'.

qa.q: What can someone in Leela's place take from Seema's thanks?
qa.a: They can accept thanks simply and know that a small stand, and being seen, can matter more than any speech.

qa.q: What stayed with Seema most, according to Leela?
qa.a: What stayed with Seema was that somebody turned around and saw her.

grounding: A defended student thanks the defender quietly, and the defender learns that being seen can matter more than any speech.

passage: Afreen had forgotten about the canteen incident until Rafiq stopped her on the Andheri station staircase on Friday. The week before, when some boys mocked his lisp as he ordered samosas, she had simply said, 'Let him order,' and stood beside him until they drifted off. Now he held out a folded paper. 'I'm bad at saying things,' he said, not quite looking at her. 'So I wrote it.' The note said: 'Thank you for seeing me. Nobody's done that since I joined.' Afreen's first instinct was to wave it off: it was nothing, anyone would have. She stopped herself. 'Thank you for telling me,' she said instead, and tucked the note into her ID card cover. Rafiq smiled, relief all over his face. On the train home she read it again. She'd said three words. They had mattered more than she'd guessed.

qa.q: Where did Afreen keep Rafiq's note?
How did Afreen feel reading the note on the train home?
qa.a: She felt moved and a little surprised that three words had mattered so much 😊

qa.q: Why was saying 'Thank you for telling me' better than waving it off?
qa.a: It accepted Rafiq's gratitude and honoured his effort to write it, instead of shrinking what he felt.

qa.q: What did Afreen's stand mean to Rafiq?
qa.a: It made him feel seen for the first time since he joined, which is why he wrote the note.

grounding: Shows a teen quietly thanked by a classmate she defended, choosing to accept it and realising being seen mattered to him.

passage:
'Darshan, wait up.' Eshaan jogged across the nets, bat under his arm.
'What's up?'
'Nothing. Just... that thing in the group chat. When they kept calling me "chipmunk" and you wrote "Enough, guys."'
'Oh. That was nothing.'
'It wasn't nothing.' Eshaan scuffed the ground. 'Everyone else sent laughing faces. You were the only one.'
Darshan opened his mouth to say anyone would've done it, then closed it. 'Okay,' he said. 'I'm glad it helped.'
'It did. My mum noticed I stopped hiding my phone at dinner.'
'Did they stop?'
'Mostly. Two of them even said sorry.'
'Good.' Darshan tapped his bat against Eshaan's pad. 'You can tell me if it starts again.'
'I know. That's kind of the point.' Eshaan grinned. 'Also, you owe me a net session. You got me out twice last week.'
'Deal. Tomorrow, six o'clock.'

qa.q: What did Darshan write in the group chat?
What was Darshan feeling when Eshaan thanked him?
qa.a: He felt a little awkward and tempted to brush it off, then glad his words had helped.

qa.q: What did Darshan do right in this conversation?
qa.a: He accepted the thanks instead of dismissing it, and offered to be there if the teasing starts again.

qa.q: How did Darshan's message change things for Eshaan?
qa.a: Eshaan felt less alone and stopped hiding his phone at dinner, since one person had stood with him.

grounding: Shows a teen thanked quietly by a classmate he defended online, accepting the thanks and learning that being seen mattered.
